plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single isometric line drawing of a rectangular block subdivided into unit cells, drawn entirely in salmon-red strokes on white. The block reads as a stack of small cubes: the front face is ruled into a four-by-four arrangement of square cells, and the visible top and right-hand faces are ruled into matching grids receding from the viewer, so an interior lattice is implied throughout. Three black dimension bars with serif end caps mark the extents. A vertical bar along the left edge is labeled H, a bar beneath the lower-left edge is labeled W, and a bar beneath the lower-right edge, receding away from the viewer, is labeled C. Near the back of the top face one cell is drawn displaced from the surface, isolating a single unit cube, and a white square panel with a thin black border and a soft drop shadow floats just above it carrying the boldface letter X. Ruling the volume into addressable cells rather than drawing a smooth solid keeps every entry individually locatable by its three coordinates. The picture gives a concrete spatial reading of a three-axis tensor whose dimensions are channels, height, and width, the shape used to hold a color image.

elements: wireframe block of salmon-red edges, 4 (W) x 4 (H) x 4 (C) unit cells
4x4 grid lines ruling the front face (W by H)
4x4 grid lines ruling the top face (W by C)
4x4 grid lines ruling the right face (C by H)
64 individually addressable unit cube cells
vertical dimension bar with serif end caps on the left, labeled H
dimension bar beneath the front bottom edge, parallel to W, labeled W
dimension bar beneath the right bottom edge, receding along C, labeled C
one displaced unit cube lifted off the top face near its back (the X cell)
floating white square panel with thin black border and soft drop shadow, carrying bold serif X

interactions.label: Channel (C) slice
interactions.teaches: Sweeping along the C axis highlights one full H-by-W sheet at a time, showing that a color-image tensor is a stack of aligned spatial maps, one per channel
Hovering a unit cell reveals its (C, H, W) index triple and lifts it clear of the surface like the marked X cell, tying one stored value to its exact location in the volume
Rotating the block confirms that H, W, and C are three mutually perpendicular axes — vertical, screen-right, and receding depth — so the volume is genuinely 3D, not a stack of 2D pictures

demo_steps.title: The front channel sheet
demo_steps.narration: With the slice at C = 1, the front-most H-by-W sheet is highlighted: each channel is one complete spatial map over the image plane.

demo_steps.title: Sweep through depth
demo_steps.narration: Dragging toward C = 4 moves the highlighted sheet through the volume — the same H-by-W pattern re-addressed at each depth position along the channel axis.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Block spans W=4 along +X (screen-right), H=4 along +Y (up), C=4 along +Z (receding); unit cell edge = 1 world unit, so the block is 4x4x4 and occupies x,y,z in [0,4]. The front face (z=0) shows the W-by-H 4x4 grid, the right face (x=4) the C-by-H grid, the top face (y=4) the W-by-C grid — surface rulings only, no interior lines. Draw as salmon-red line strokes ~#ee655c on white, no filled faces except hover/active-sheet highlights. Lifted X cell sits on the top face at roughly W index 3, C index 3 (1-based from the front-left), raised ~0.5 units above y=4. X panel: white square ~1.3 units, thin black border, offset grey drop-shadow copy behind it, bold black serif 'X', held just above the lifted cell. H bar: vertical line at x ~ -1, spanning y=0..4, with short horizontal serif end caps; label 'H' to its left at mid-height. W bar: below the front bottom edge (z=0, y ~ -1), parallel to +X spanning x=0..4, caps at both ends, label 'W' beneath its midpoint. C bar: below the right bottom edge (x=4, y ~ -1), parallel to +Z spanning z=0..4, label 'C' beneath its midpoint. Bars and labels are black; labels in italic serif. Active channel sheet = all cells with depth index c-1, shown with a translucent salmon fill (~0.25 opacity) plus a thicker outline.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the three surface grids as one THREE.LineSegments lattice (draw the three visible faces' rulings and outer edges; interior cells are never drawn). Use 64 individual BoxGeometry meshes (or an InstancedMesh with per-instance ids) purely for raycasting — keep them invisible except when hovered or part of the active sheet. Hover: raise the cell ~0.5 units along its nearest surface normal (top cells up, front cells toward viewer, right cells rightward) and show a sprite label '(C, H, W) = (c, h, w)'. The X cell is a permanently raised mesh with its panel as a canvas-texture sprite plus a translated darker sprite behind for the drop shadow. Dimension bars are lines with short perpendicular cap ticks and sprite labels. Slider moves the highlight fill along +Z; highlight the sheet edges thicker for contrast. Standard isometric camera pose; orbit limited so the three ruled faces stay the readable ones.

- Slider for sweeping a channel slice along C; the active H by W sheet highlights one depth position at a time, showing how a color image tensor stores multiple aligned spatial maps.

authoredContext:
This example shows the basic concept of working with tensors and batches
for one-dimensional data, but, in vision, most of the time we will be
working with higher-dimensional tensors. For image data we typically use
four-dimensional tensors: batch $\times$ channels $\times$ height
$\times$ width; for videos we may use five-dimensional tensors: batch
$\times$ channels $\times$ height $\times$ width $\times$ time.
Three-dimensional (3D) scans have an additional depth spatial
dimension; videos of 3D data could therefore be represented by
six-dimensional tensors. As you can see, thinking in terms of
two-dimensional matrices is not quite sufficient. Instead, you should be
imagining data processing as operating on $N$-dimensional tensors,
sliced and diced in different ways. As a step in this direction, you may
find it useful to visualize tensors in 3D, as shown in
the figure.

A 3D tensor that could represent an $C \times H \times W$ color image.

discrepancies: Source grid lines are thick bold salmon strokes; the generated lattice is thin hairlines, weakening the visual match
The X panel floats noticeably above the top face on a raised wireframe cell, while in the source it sits directly on the top face
A translucent pink highlighted sheet fills the front face by default, which does not appear in the source figure
The X panel is rendered as a billboard sprite rather than lying flat on the top face plane as in the source
evaluation.notes: Correct 4x4x4 salmon lattice cube with H/W/C dimension bars and X label, plus rich channel-slice slider, demo steps, and hover indexing; minor mismatches in line weight, X panel placement, and the default highlighted sheet.
action_items: Thicken the lattice lines (e.g. cylinder edges or fat lines) to match the bold salmon strokes of the source
Rest the X panel flat on the top face instead of floating it above a raised cell
Hide the translucent channel sheet in the default state so the initial view matches the clean source cube

feedback.rationale: Concept accuracy and interactivity are perfect (5s), overall average is 4.6, and remaining discrepancies are minor visual polish (line weight, panel offset, default sheet visibility) that don't impede understanding.
